Description: Full 16-year hourly electricity demand for PJM East showing overall trend and seasonal cycles from 2002 to 2018
Breaks PJM demand into three components — long-term trend (rising demand) + weekly seasonality + random residual noise
Autocorrelation analysis confirming strong dependencies at lag 1 hour lag 24 hours and lag 168 hours (one week) justifying the 24-hour window choice
Average electricity demand grouped by hour of day day of week and month showing when demand peaks and drops
Grid showing average demand by hour vs day of week — darkest cells reveal the highest-demand time slots across the week
7-day rolling mean and standard deviation over time showing how demand variability changes across seasons and years
Overlay of actual electricity demand and predictions from all 5 models on the test set showing how closely each model tracks real values
Bar chart comparing RMSE MAE MAPE and R² across all 5 models — Random Forest is the clear winner on every metric
Radar (spider) chart normalising all 4 metrics onto one plot — larger area means better overall performance across all metrics
Training loss vs validation loss per epoch for LSTM GRU and CNN-LSTM showing how each model converged during training
Full 4-year hourly household power consumption for the UCI dataset showing the erratic and unpredictable nature of residential usage
Breaks UCI household consumption into trend seasonality and residual — residual is much larger than for PJM showing higher randomness
Autocorrelation analysis for UCI household data confirming similar lag patterns to PJM but with weaker correlations due to individual behaviour
Average household power usage grouped by hour of day day of week and month showing morning and evening peaks from appliance use
Grid of average household power consumption by hour vs day of week showing evening peaks when residents return home
Heatmap showing how strongly each of the 7 sub-metering channels correlates with each other — darker = stronger relationship
Overlay of actual household consumption and model predictions — wider gaps compared to PJM reflect the difficulty of forecasting household data
Bar chart comparing all 5 models on UCI dataset — XGBoost edges Random Forest while all deep learning models perform significantly worse
Radar chart for UCI dataset showing Random Forest and XGBoost dominating deep learning models across all metrics
